title: First line of a TikTok: 36 hooks that stop the swipe

# First line of a TikTok: 36 hooks that stop the swipe

At 0:00, your video opens with “Hey guys, today I want to talk about my morning routine.” Before the second sentence lands, the viewer has moved on.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

The first line of a TikTok has one job: make the next second feel more valuable than the swipe. This guide gives you ready-to-use opening lines, plus a way to choose one that fits the video you actually made.

## First lines for fitness TikToks

1. “Stop going to the gym every day.”
2. “The gym isn’t the problem—your first week is.”
3. “If you keep quitting workouts, start here.”
4. “This is the beginner mistake that makes exercise feel impossible.”
5. “You do not need a harder workout; you need this smaller rule.”
6. “I’d change this one thing before buying another fitness program.”

## First lines for money and career TikToks

7. “Before you ask for a raise, check this.”
8. “Most budgets fail before the first purchase.”
9. “I stopped treating this as a productivity problem.”
10. “If your paycheck disappears by [ADD: your date], try this first.”
11. “This job-search advice sounds smart and wastes your time.”
12. “Here’s the sentence I’d remove from your résumé today.”

## First lines for beauty and style TikToks

13. “This is why that makeup look looks different on you.”
14. “Do this before you buy another skincare product.”
15. “Your closet may not need more clothes.”
16. “I tested the order of these two steps so you do not have to.”
17. “The problem is not your outfit—it’s this proportion.”
18. “If your sunscreen pills, check what you put on first.”

## First lines for food TikToks

19. “Do not start this recipe until you see the last ingredient.”
20. “This is the weeknight dinner I make when nothing sounds good.”
21. “Your scrambled eggs are probably cooking too long.”
22. “I made this with [ADD: number] ingredients and one pan.”
23. “The sauce is not the secret; this first step is.”
24. “If your rice keeps turning out wrong, change this one habit.”

## First lines for travel and local-guide TikToks

25. “Skip the place everyone films and go here instead.”
26. “This is what [ADD: your budget] gets you for one day here.”
27. “I planned this trip around one mistake I did not want to repeat.”
28. “Do not book that hotel until you check this.”
29. “Here’s the first thing I would do with one afternoon in [ADD: place].”
30. “This itinerary only works if you start with this stop.”

## First lines for education and how-to TikToks

31. “You do not need to memorize this; you need to see the pattern.”
32. “Here’s the part nobody explains before you start.”
33. “If this topic confuses you, begin with this picture.”
34. “I can explain [ADD: topic] without using the usual jargon.”
35. “This looks like a small detail until you see what it changes.”
36. “You can fix this in [ADD: your time], but only in this order.”

## Pick a first line that matches the video

Choose the promise before choosing the wording. A good opening makes a specific promise that the rest of the video can keep.

- Use a **contrarian line** when the video overturns familiar advice: “Stop going to the gym every day.”
- Use a **question** when the viewer already feels the problem: “Why does everyone quit by January 20th?”
- Use a **mistake line** when you can identify a fix quickly: “You’re not lazy. You’re doing week one wrong.”
- Use a **specific result line** only when you can show the real number or process in the video.
- Use a **scene-setting line** when the visual itself creates curiosity: “I planned this trip around one mistake I did not want to repeat.”

Avoid opening with a label—“three tips,” “a day in my life,” or “come with me”—unless the following image supplies a clear reason to stay. The viewer needs the tension, not the category.

## Test the line before you film the whole thing

Write three versions of the same opening: one contrarian, one question, and one mistake. Read each aloud over the first shot. Keep the one that is easiest to understand without sound, matches the on-screen text, and leads naturally into your next sentence.

Then make the first three seconds earn the claim. If the spoken line says there is a mistake, show the mistake or name it immediately. If it makes a promise, give the viewer the first piece of the answer before the video drifts into setup.

A practical script shape is simple: 0–3 seconds, the hook; 3–10 seconds, name the tension or mistake; 10 seconds onward, deliver the useful part; close with the next action.

One of the easiest first lines to test is a question the viewer is already asking; see [question hooks for TikTok](https://aniccaai.com/blog/question-hooks-for-tiktok?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=related_links_1101) for examples and when they backfire.


Related guide: [First Line of a Reel: 35 Ready-to-Film Hooks That Stop the Swipe](https://aniccaai.com/blog/first-line-of-a-reel?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=related_links_1102b)

## FAQ

### How long should the first line of a TikTok be?

Short enough to understand on the first listen. If it needs multiple clauses to make sense, make the claim smaller or move the qualification into the next line.

### Should the spoken line and on-screen text be identical?

They can be, but they do not have to be. Let the spoken line carry the natural voice and let the text make the main promise easy to scan.

### Can I reuse a first-line format?

Yes. Reuse the structure when it still matches the video; change the actual promise, evidence, and visual so viewers receive something real rather than a repeated shell.

### What if my topic is boring?

Do not call it boring. Find the costly mistake, surprising contrast, difficult choice, or practical outcome inside it. The hook should be accurate, not louder than the video can support.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the format it produces:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
